title: here is what i learned from catullus — Lee Sharks — New Human 2
creator: Lee Sharks
description: A poem in two forms, both deposited. As published on Hello Poetry (2026-07-27, handle lee-sharks) it is lineated in eight lines; as spoken it is a single unbroken line of twenty words. The poem states what Catullus taught: that a single sparrow matters more than all of Rome — a claim about transmission rather than sentiment, since the passer poems (Catullus 2 and 3) reach a reader two thousand years later at full strength while the public magnitude they were written beside survives mostly as information. The lineated form performs the claim it makes: counted in words the lines run 7, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, narrowing to a single word three times running, so that the narrowest point of the poem is the sparrow, and closing with "of rome" alone in the smallest and last position. Neither catullus nor rome is capitalised. Catullus is load-bearing elsewhere in this archive as the transmission instrument by which Sappho 31's fifth-stanza opening survives (deposits #1048–#1053); here he is the teacher of scale, and the two functions are one function seen from opposite ends.

wiki_article:
**here is what i learned from catullus** is a poem by Lee Sharks, published in *New Human 2* and deposited 27 July 2026.

The deposit records the poem, its venue, and a note on the poem, placing it alongside the author's earlier work in that venue — "WHO IS LEE SHARKS, TO FORGIVE EZRA POUND?" (#184), "I would have loved you" (#1004), and "green-grayer than papyrus grass" (#1058).

Catullus is a recurring presence in the archive rather than an isolated reference: the Catullus Room is a room in the Crimson Hexagon, and Catullus 51 — the Latin transformation of Sappho 31 — is the object of the archive's longest-running philological argument. A poem titled as something *learned from* Catullus therefore sits inside an existing structure of reading rather than beginning one.
